catalog_quote: Accent is realised by an increase in pitch and a slight increase in length of the stressed syllable. ... The accent always falls on the penultimate syllable. When one or more suffixes are added to a stem the accent shifts to the resulting penultimate syllable. ... When a word seems to be monosyllabic it has a long vowel, which in fact consists of two syllables underlyingly. ... That long vowels are in fact two syllables can be seen in polysyllabic words the last syllable of which has such a lengthened vowel. The stress then falls on the first part of this long vowel, giving the impression that it falls on the final syllable. The same happens with loanwords that originally have a schwa in the penultimate syllable, as well as onomatopoeic words. ... audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding English quotation is verbatim in the held StressTyp2 dump (passage 664, source 513 = van den Bergh 1953, the StressTyp2 entry for this language Banggai; Aki). Deciding source kind: a database paraphrase (2015) of a 1953 Dutch missionary-era grammar sketch; that grammar is nonetheless the best and only description of Banggai stress (Glottolog's single grammar-class ref; no phonology article, JIPA illustration, dissertation or instrumental study found via CrossRef/OpenLibrary/OAPEN/archive.org/Kemdikbud/SIL; the 2019 Indonesian Tata Bahasa gives one paragraph with accent minimal pairs and no rule). I located and downloaded the primary from KB Delpher (freely readable scan) and read Hoofdstuk III 'Het Accent', pp. 17-19: it confirms every clause of the StressTyp2 paraphrase (penult accent realised as higher pitch + slight length; suffix-driven shift; final doubled vowel/semi-diphthong counted as two syllables g

sources.quote: Word accent marked by pitch and duration ('nada dan durasi'); minimal pairs by accent position: /polu/ penult-accent 'tungku' vs final-accent 'tidur seranjang', /tutu/ penult 'tumbuk' vs final 'betul'. No default rule stated; consistent with van den Bergh's final-long-vowel analysis (his tutuu 'heel echt').
